title: Module 4 · Lesson 3 — Resilience: keeping agents alive when things break

lines: Welcome to lesson three: keeping agents alive when things break.
An agent relies on a model, tools, and data stores, and any of them can fail.
Picture a travel agent rebooking passengers after a storm cancels hundreds of flights.
Then the airline's seat-availability service slows to a crawl.
Every rebooking hangs on that one service, until no workers are left.
Now even passengers who only wanted a hotel get nothing.
The first pattern is a timeout on every external call, shorter than the caller's budget.
A tool with no timeout can hang an agent run forever.
The second is bounded retries: backoff with jitter, capped attempts, and only for transient errors.
Never retry a four-hundred-class error, because wrong arguments stay wrong.
The third is a circuit breaker: after repeated failures, stop calling and fail fast for a cool-down.
That way, one slow service can't swallow every worker.
The fourth is bulkheads: a separate connection pool for each dependency.
If the seat service fills its pool, hotel and baggage requests still flow.
Beware the retry storm, where the agent retries while its HTTP client retries too.
Let one layer own retries, make side-effecting tools idempotent, and always add jitter.
When the seat service is down, degrade gracefully instead of erroring or making something up.
Serve cached seats with their age shown, or fall back to a smaller model.
Failing that, answer a narrower question, queue the request, or hand off to a human.
The one unacceptable behavior is answering as if nothing were wrong.
Keep session state in Redis or Postgres, so any replica can serve any request.
That beats sticky sessions, which break when pods scale down.
Checkpoint after each significant step, so a crashed run resumes instead of restarting.
And give every run a durable ID, so a complaint traces to its exact path.
For high availability, run inference in two regions and keep a backup model provider.
Replicate the vector index, and test failover, because untested failover is just a hypothesis.
On the exam, the complete answer names a timeout, bounded retries with jitter, a circuit breaker, and a fallback.
Retries alone are the trap, so read on for the details.
